one_liner: Hand-tuned sm_86 CUDA/SASS ML kernels; FP16 HGEMM roughly ties cuBLAS on one laptop GPU, other kernels trail vendor libraries.
what_it_does: A research corpus of ML kernels (SGEMM/HGEMM, 2:4 sparse HGEMM, INT8 IGEMM, Flash Attention, implicit-GEMM conv2d, softmax/layernorm/groupnorm, activations) written for one GPU, the RTX 3070 Ti Laptop (GA104, sm_86). Each kernel is an extern "C" __global__ function compiled to a .cubin and driven by a CUDA Driver API bench, optionally byte-patched at SASS level with the project's R package cuasmR. It is not a library with a BLAS-style API: hgemm_16warp takes row-major FP16 A and B and writes row-major FP32 C with no alpha/beta, transpose or stream arguments.
how_it_is_fast: hgemm_16warp uses a 128x128 block tile with 16 warps in a 4x4 grid, each warp owning a 2x2 set of 16x16 WMMA tiles, so accumulators drop to 32 registers and __launch_bounds__(512, 2) fits two blocks (32 warps) per SM. A and B tiles are double-buffered in shared memory with cp.async (LDGSTS, 16-byte copies), padded by 8 halves per row to avoid bank conflicts, and kept under the 50 KB per-block shared-memory cliff that the project measured as a 2x cliff on GA104. The docs frame the work as 'four laws of GA104': feed the Tensor Cores, read each DRAM byte once, fill the warp schedulers, stay under 50 KB of shared memory.
when_to_use: Learning how an Ampere tensor-core GEMM is built from WMMA, cp.async double buffering and occupancy tuning, with a documented phase-by-phase progression (naive SGEMM 1.0x to HGEMM 16-warp 69.2x to sparse 2:4 90.5x in docs/inventory.md).
Studying SASS-level editing on sm_86: the cuasmR workflow (cubin to nvdisasm to byte patch) and the tutorial chapters are the distinctive part of the repo.
Square FP16-in/FP32-out GEMMs at 2048^3 to 4096^3 on a GA104 (RTX 3070 Ti class) card where you want a small, readable kernel that lands within a few percent of cuBLAS.
Reusing its benchmark discipline: the clock-lock, throttle-rejection and baseline-provenance rules in data/baselines.json and AGENTS.md are a useful template for noisy laptop GPUs.
when_not_to_use: Production GEMM on any GPU other than sm_86: kernels, constants and tuning target GA104 only, and the repo has no CI that runs on a GPU.

When you need a measurable win over cuBLAS: under the project's own clock-locked baselines HGEMM is about 1.02x cuBLAS, and at native boost it measured 28,090 and 27,307 GFLOPS, below the recorded cuBLAS reference (28,631 and 29,708).
INT8, sparse INT8 and convolution: the project's own table shows IGEMM at 68.7% of cuBLAS, sparse IGEMM at 25.4% and 18.2% of cuSPARSELt, and conv2d at 42.3% of cuDNN.
General shapes or layouts: the HGEMM kernel has no transpose, alpha/beta or batched variants and skips any 16x16 output tile that crosses the M/N boundary.
Teams without R and the Windows/WSL2 setup: make reproduce needs CUDA 13.2, R 4.6.0 with renv and the local cuasmR package.

integration.dependencies: CUDA toolkit (CUDA 13.2 documented) and the CUDA Driver API for benches; R 4.6.0 with renv packages and the local cuasmR package for the build/bench/SASS-patch tooling; cuBLAS, cuBLASLt, cuDNN and cuSPARSELt only for the reference benches
integration.min_toolchain: nvcc -arch=sm_86 -O2 (Makefile); documented toolchain CUDA 13.2 (nvcc V13.2.78), R 4.6.0; older CUDA versions not documented
integration.platforms: NVIDIA sm_86 (GA104, RTX 3070 Ti Laptop) only; developed under WSL2 on a Windows host
integration.thread_safety: not documented (plain kernels with no global state; launch and stream handling is up to the caller)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false - kernels are raw extern "C" cubin entry points with fixed row-major FP16 x FP16 -> FP32 semantics, not a cublasGemmEx-compatible API

gotchas: hgemm_16warp silently skips writing any 16x16 output tile that would cross the M or N edge, and its 16-byte cp.async loads assume rows aligned to 8 halves; use M and N that are multiples of 16 and K, N multiples of 8 (read from the kernel source, not documented as a contract).

Benchmark numbers depend on clock regime: issue #158 (open) records hgemm_16warp running about 10% slower at native boost than under a 1605 MHz lock, and #159 (open) records two locked sessions disagreeing by 4.9% on the 4096^3 figure.

The 31,875/31,765 GFLOPS rows in docs/comparison_to_sota.md and the 31,910 headline in docs/inventory.md are native-boost readings the project itself footnotes as disputed (#167, closed by PR #206); the cuBLAS reference was recorded on 2026-05-18 without a clock lock, so the comparison mixes dates and regimes.
Bench executables load cubins by relative filename and must be run from their own directory (AGENTS.md).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over fast.cu when your hardware is a consumer Ampere card (sm_86) rather than an H100, or when the goal is learning SASS-level tuning; fast.cu shows a larger and better-documented margin over cuBLAS (about 1.07x at N=4096 on H100). FastGEMV covers matrix-vector (memory-bound) work, not GEMM, so the two do not overlap.
verified_claims_summary: On an RTX 3070 Ti Laptop GPU (150 W cap, WSL2, CUDA 13.2, nvcc -O2 sm_86), the 16-warp FP16 HGEMM at 2048^3 and 4096^3 was compared with a local cublasGemmEx harness (FP16 in, FP32 out, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F_FAST_16F, median of 11 after 5 warmups). The current clock-locked project baselines (29,174 and 30,401 GFLOPS) sit about 2% above the cuBLAS readings (28,631 and 29,708), a margin smaller than the project's own 4.9% session-to-session spread; the 107-111% figures on the comparison page are older native-boost readings.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-08-17, 2 stars, MIT), with unusually candid self-auditing in its issue tracker; usable as copyable reference code for sm_86, not as a maintained GEMM library.
